## Importing Attribute Data into R





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
popdata <- read_csv("data/aspatial/respopagesextod2011to2020.csv")
```
:::






## Data Preparation

### Data wrangling





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
popdata2020 <- popdata %>%
  filter(Time == 2020) %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from=AG, 
              values_from=POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[3:6])
         +rowSums(.[12])) %>%
mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(.[7:11])+
rowSums(.[13:15]))%>%
mutate(`AGED`=rowSums(.[16:21])) %>%
mutate(`TOTAL`=rowSums(.[3:21])) %>%  
mutate(`DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`)
/`ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, 
       `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`, 
       `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)
```
:::






### Joining the attribute data and geospatial data





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
popdata2020 <- popdata2020 %>%
  mutate(across(c(PA, SZ), toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mpsz_pop2020 <- left_join(mpsz, popdata2020,
                          by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
write_rds(mpsz_pop2020, "data/rds/mpszpop2020.rds")
```
:::






# Choropleth Mapping Geospatial Data Using tmap

## Plotting a choropleth map quickly by using `qtm()`





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tmap_mode("plot")
qtm(mpsz_pop2020, 
    fill = "DEPENDENCY")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::






## Creating a choropleth map by using tmap’s elements

While `qtm()` is quick for choropleth maps, it limits aesthetic control, so using `tmap` elements is better for high-quality cartography.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_grid(alpha =0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authorithy (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics DOS", 
             position = c("left", "bottom"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::






### Drawing a Base Map

`tmap` maps start with `tm_shape()` to define the data, followed by layers like `tm_polygons()` to draw features such as planning subzones.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::






### Drawing a choropleth map using tm_polygons()

To create a choropleth map by planning subzone, assign the target variable (e.g., Dependency) to `tm_polygons()`.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::






### Drawing a choropleth map using **tm_fill()** and **tm_border()**

`tm_polygons()` is a wrapper for `tm_fill()` and `tm_borders()`; using `tm_fill()` alone shades polygons based on a variable with the default color scheme.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::






The subzones are shaded by their dependency values; to add their boundaries, use tm_borders() as shown below.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.01,  
             fill_alpha = 0.1)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::






## Data classification methods of tmap

Most choropleth maps employ some methods of data classification. The point of classification is to take a large number of observations and group them into data ranges or classes.

tmap provides a total ten data classification methods, namely: fixed, sd, equal, pretty (default), quantile, kmeans, hclust, bclust, fisher, and jenks.

To define a data classification method, the style argument of tm_fill() or tm_polygons() will be used.

### Plotting choropleth maps with built-in classification methods

The code chunk below shows a quantile data classification that used 5 classes. 





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "jenks",
        n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::






In the code chunk below, equal data classification method is used.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "equal",
        n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::






## DIY Using Quantile Classification Method (20 Classes)





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 20),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_grid(alpha =0.2) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA)\nand Population data from Department of Statistics DOS", 
             position = c("left", "bottom"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::






### Plotting choropleth map with custome break





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(mpsz_pop2020$DEPENDENCY)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
 0.1111  0.7147  0.7867  0.8585  0.8763 19.0000      92 
```


:::
:::





We set custom breaks as `c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00)` and use them to plot the choropleth map with manual classification.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
          breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::






## Colour Scheme

`tmap` supports colour ramps either defined by the user or a set of predefined colour ramps from the `RColorBrewer` package.

### Using ColourBrewer palette

To change the colour, we assign the preferred colour to values argument of `tm_scale_intervals()` as shown in the code chunk below.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "quantile",
        n = 5,
        values = "brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::






Notice that the choropleth map is shaded in green.

To reverse the colour shading, add a “-” prefix.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "quantile",
        n = 5,
        values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::






## Map Layout

Map layout combines all elements—such as the map objects, title, scale bar, compass, margins, and aspect ratio—into a cohesive visual, with color settings and classification methods influencing its overall appearance.

###  Map Legend
In tmap, several `tm_legend()` options are provided to change the placement, format and appearance of the legend.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "jenks",
        n = 5,
        values = "brewer.greens"),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone \n(Jenks classification)")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::






###  Map style
tmap allows a wide variety of layout settings to be changed. They can be called by using tmap_style().

The code chunk below shows the classic style is used.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY", 
          style = "quantile", 
          palette = "-Greens") +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("classic")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::






### Cartographic Furniture
Beside map style, tmap also also provides arguments to draw other map furniture such as compass, scale bar and grid lines.

In the code chunk below, tm_compass(), tm_scale_bar() and tm_grid() are used to add compass, scale bar and grid lines onto the choropleth map.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_grid(alpha =0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authorithy (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics DOS", 
             position = c("left", "bottom"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::






To reset the default style, refer to the code chunk below.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tmap_style("white")
```
:::






## Drawing Small Multiple Choropleth Maps

Small multiple maps in `tmap` can be created by mapping multiple values to aesthetics, using `tm_facets()`, or combining maps with `tmap_arrange()`.

### By assigning multiple values to at least one of the aesthetic arguments

In this example, small multiple choropleth maps are created by defining ncols in `tm_fill()`





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_fill(c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
          style = "equal", 
          palette = "Blues") +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("right", "bottom")) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("white")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::





In this example, small multiple choropleth maps are created by assigning multiple values to at least one of the aesthetic arguments





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+ 
  tm_polygons(c("DEPENDENCY","AGED"),
          style = c("equal", "quantile"), 
          palette = list("Blues","Greens")) +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("right", "bottom"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::






###  By defining a group-by variable in tm_facets()
In this example, multiple small choropleth maps are created by using `tm_facets()`.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          style = "quantile",
          palette = "Blues",
          thres.poly = 0) + 
  tm_facets(by="REGION_N", 
            free.coords=TRUE) +
  tm_layout(legend.show = FALSE,
            title.position = c("center", "center"), 
            title.size = 20) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::





### By creating multiple stand-alone maps with tmap_arrange()

In this example, multiple small choropleth maps are created by creating multiple stand-alone maps with tmap_arrange().





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
youngmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+ 
  tm_polygons("YOUNG", 
              style = "quantile", 
              palette = "Blues")

agedmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+ 
  tm_polygons("AGED", 
              style = "quantile", 
              palette = "Blues")

tmap_arrange(youngmap, agedmap, asp=1, ncol=2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::






## Mappping Spatial Object Meeting a Selection Criterion

Instead of creating small multiple choropleth map, you can also use selection funtion to map spatial objects meeting the selection criterion.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020[mpsz_pop2020$REGION_N=="CENTRAL REGION", ])+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY", 
          style = "quantile", 
          palette = "Blues", 
          legend.hist = TRUE, 
          legend.is.portrait = TRUE,
          legend.hist.z = 0.1) +
  tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE,
            legend.height = 0.45, 
            legend.width = 5.0,
            legend.position = c("right", "bottom"),
            frame = FALSE) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08-01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-30-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::
